interactions.label: Why is checking for IMNCI general danger signs the first step in evaluating ever

params.question: Why is checking for IMNCI general danger signs the first step in evaluating every febrile child, before taking a detailed history?

answers.text: Because danger signs are found more frequently than other clinical features in febrile children

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Danger signs are not common, but their presence signals life-threatening illness. Their priority comes from urgency, not frequency.

answers.text: Because any single danger sign demands immediate resuscitation and referral, overriding all other assessment steps

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A child who is unable to drink, vomiting everything, convulsing, lethargic, unconscious, or has a stiff neck needs resuscitation and referral before any further workup.

answers.text: Because danger signs identify the specific causative organism responsible for the fever

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Danger signs (lethargy, inability to drink, convulsions, stiff neck) indicate severity, not aetiology. Identifying the organism comes later through history and investigation.

answers.text: Because the IMNCI protocol requires the entire assessment to be completed in under 30 seconds

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 30-second check is a rapid screening for danger signs only. The full IMNCI assessment includes a detailed history and examination beyond those initial 30 seconds.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the rationale for checking danger signs first is that any single one (unable to drink, vomiting everything, convulsions, lethargy/unconsciousness, stiff neck) indicates a life-threatening condition requiring immediate action — it overrides all other steps.
Well done. The 30-second danger-sign check is the gatekeeper of the systematic approach: if any danger sign is present, you resuscitate and refer before anything else.

interactions.label: Which clinical finding most reliably distinguishes the pharyngeal membrane of di

params.question: Which clinical finding most reliably distinguishes the pharyngeal membrane of diphtheria from the tonsillar exudate of streptococcal infection?

answers.text: Presence of high-grade fever with a sore throat

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both diphtheria and streptococcal tonsillitis present with fever and sore throat. Fever is actually often only low-grade in diphtheria, unlike the high fever of streptococcal pharyngitis.

answers.text: The membrane extends beyond the tonsillar pillars and bleeds when scraped off

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The diphtheritic pseudomembrane characteristically spreads beyond the tonsillar pillars (unlike streptococcal exudate that stays within them) and bleeds on attempted removal — the key bedside differentiator.

answers.text: Tender, enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cervical lymphadenopathy occurs in both conditions. In diphtheria, extensive glandular and soft-tissue swelling produces a 'bull neck', but lymph node enlargement alone does not distinguish the two.

answers.text: A muffled 'hot potato' voice with difficulty swallowing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A muffled voice can occur in both severe tonsillitis (particularly peritonsillar abscess) and diphtheria. It is suggestive but not the most reliable distinguishing feature.

overallFeedback.feedback: The diphtheritic pseudomembrane has two features that set it apart: it extends beyond the tonsillar pillars, and it bleeds when you try to scrape it off. Streptococcal exudate stays within the tonsillar pillars and wipes off cleanly.
Exactly. The two cardinal signs of the diphtheritic membrane are extension beyond the tonsillar pillars and bleeding on removal — both absent in simple streptococcal exudate.

interactions.label: A child with suspected enteric fever has sustained high fever, lethargy, hepatos

params.question: A child with suspected enteric fever has sustained high fever, lethargy, hepatosplenomegaly, and faint salmon-pink spots on the abdomen that fade on pressure. Which stage of the illness does this clinical picture most likely represent?

answers.text: Week 1 — the stepladder fever phase with constipation and rising temperature

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Week 1 is characterised by gradually rising fever (stepladder pattern), headache, malaise, and constipation. Hepatosplenomegaly and rose spots have not yet appeared at this stage.

answers.text: Week 2 — peak systemic toxaemia with hepatosplenomegaly and rose spots

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. By week 2, fever plateaus at 39–40°C, the child appears toxic with lethargy (typhoid encephalopathy in severe cases), hepatosplenomegaly is established, and rose spots appear on the trunk in 10–20% of patients.

answers.text: Week 3 — the complication phase with peak risk of intestinal perforation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Week 3 carries the highest risk of intestinal perforation and bleeding from necrosis of Peyer's patches. While fever may start settling, rose spots typically appear during week 2, not week 3.

answers.text: Convalescent phase — as fever settles and the child begins to recover

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: During convalescence, systemic signs are resolving. The combination of sustained high fever, toxaemia, and fresh rose spots indicates active disease at its peak, not recovery.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the weekly progression: Week 1 = stepladder fever, constipation, relative bradycardia. Week 2 = sustained high fever, toxaemia, hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots. Week 3 = complication peak (perforation, bleeding). Match the clinical findings to the stage.
Well done. The combination of sustained high fever, systemic toxaemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and rose spots is the hallmark of week 2 of typhoid, when Salmonella Typhi bacteraemia peaks.

interactions.label: A child with dengue fever appears to be improving as the fever settles on day 4.

params.question: A child with dengue fever appears to be improving as the fever settles on day 4. Why is this period of defervescence the most dangerous phase of the illness?

answers.text: Viral replication peaks during defervescence, increasing viraemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Viral replication is actually highest during the febrile phase. The critical phase is driven by the host immune response causing capillary leak, not by rising viraemia.

answers.text: Capillary leak peaks as fever falls, causing plasma loss that can lead to shock

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Between days 3 and 7, as fever subsides, capillary permeability increases, causing plasma leakage. This can progress to dengue shock syndrome even as the child appears to improve clinically.

answers.text: Platelet counts rise sharply during defervescence, increasing thrombosis risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Platelet counts actually fall during the critical phase, not rise. Thrombocytopaenia contributes to the bleeding tendency seen in severe dengue.

answers.text: Secondary bacterial infection is most likely once the febrile defence subsides

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Secondary bacterial infection is not the primary danger of defervescence in dengue. The risk comes from capillary leak and plasma loss inherent to the dengue critical phase itself.

overallFeedback.feedback: In dengue, the critical phase begins as the fever comes down. Capillary leak causes plasma to shift out of blood vessels, and if unrecognised, this leads to dengue shock syndrome. Watch for warning signs even — especially — when the child appears to improve.

Exactly. The critical phase of dengue begins as fever settles (days 3–7). A child who looks better can be quietly heading toward shock from capillary leak — warning signs like abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, and rising haematocrit demand urgent review.

interactions.label: How does the diarrhoea caused by Giardia lamblia differ from that caused by Enta

params.question: How does the diarrhoea caused by Giardia lamblia differ from that caused by Entamoeba histolytica?

answers.text: Giardia causes bloody mucoid stools, while Entamoeba causes painless watery diarrhoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is reversed. Entamoeba causes bloody mucoid stools (amoebic dysentery), while Giardia produces non-bloody, fatty stools from malabsorption.

answers.text: Giardia produces chronic foul-smelling fatty stools with malabsorption, while Entamoeba causes bloody mucoid stools with tenesmus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Giardia causes chronic malabsorption with bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools (without blood or fever), while Entamoeba causes amoebic dysentery with bloody mucoid stools and straining.

answers.text: Both cause identical acute watery diarrhoea with high fever

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neither typically causes high fever. Their presentations are distinct: Giardia = chronic malabsorption with fatty stools, Entamoeba = bloody dysentery. Recognising this pattern guides investigation and treatment.

answers.text: Giardia commonly causes liver abscess, while Entamoeba remains confined to the intestine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is reversed. Entamoeba histolytica can spread beyond the gut to form amoebic liver abscesses, while Giardia lamblia stays in the small intestine causing only malabsorption.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the pattern: Giardia lamblia causes chronic malabsorption (bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools, no blood, no fever), while Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery (bloody mucoid stools, tenesmus) and can form an amoebic liver abscess.
Well done. Giardia = foul-smelling, greasy, chronic diarrhoea with malabsorption and weight loss. Entamoeba = bloody mucoid dysentery, with the potential for extra-intestinal spread to the liver.

interactions.label: A 6-year-old child with suspected dengue fever has a temperature of 40°C. Which

params.question: A 6-year-old child with suspected dengue fever has a temperature of 40°C. Which antipyretic approach is appropriate?

answers.text: Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg every 8 hours, as it provides stronger antipyretic action than paracetamol

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ibuprofen is contraindicated in suspected dengue because it increases bleeding risk. All NSAIDs must be avoided when dengue is a possibility.

answers.text: Aspirin 15 mg/kg every 6 hours for its combined anti-inflammatory and antipyretic effect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aspirin is strictly contraindicated in dengue — it inhibits platelet function and raises bleeding risk significantly. In children, it also carries the risk of Reye syndrome.

answers.text: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 4–6 hours, combined with lukewarm sponging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Paracetamol is the only safe antipyretic in suspected dengue (15 mg/kg every 4–6 hours). Lukewarm (not cold) sponging assists fever reduction without triggering shivering.

answers.text: Cold water sponging alone, without any oral antipyretic medication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cold water sponging is harmful — it triggers shivering, which paradoxically raises core body temperature. Lukewarm sponging is used alongside paracetamol, not cold water alone.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key rule in dengue management: paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 4–6 hours is the only safe antipyretic. Aspirin and ibuprofen increase bleeding risk and are contraindicated. Sponging must be lukewarm, not cold — cold water triggers shivering that paradoxically raises body temperature.
Correct. In dengue, paracetamol is the only safe antipyretic. Never aspirin, never ibuprofen — both increase bleeding risk. Sponge with lukewarm water, never cold.
